instructions: Rinse 1 1/2 cups of the rice and add it to a pot with 2 1/4 cups water. Bring it to a boil, cover, turn the heat to low and cook for 15 minutes. Leave the lid on, off the heat, until you're ready to serve.
Slice the steak across the grain, about 1/8 inch thick.
In a bowl, mix the beef with 1 tsp of the soy sauce, the cornstarch and 1 tbsp of the oil. Leave it while you prep.
Meanwhile, mince the ginger, slice the garlic thinly, and cut the scallions on an angle into 2-inch pieces.
Heat a wok or large skillet over high heat until it's smoking, then add 2 tbsp of the oil.
Add half the beef in a single layer and stir for about 45 seconds, until it's just opaque. Slightly pink in the middle is fine. Transfer it to a plate and cook the second half the same way.
Turn the heat to medium and add 2 tbsp of the oil. Add the ginger and stir for 1 minute.
Add the garlic, shacha sauce and sugar. Stir for 2 minutes, until it smells toasty and the oil looks red-brown.

Return the beef and any juices to the wok, add the scallions and the remaining 1 tbsp soy sauce, and turn the heat to high. Stir-fry for about 1 minute, until the scallions wilt and the beef is cooked through.
Taste it. If it's flat, add a pinch of salt.
method_notes: Only The Woks of Life gave a full, readable recipe for this dish (5.0 from 7 ratings, so the lead is a fallback under the 20-rating rule); Makansutra's shorter version confirms the idea. Both sear thin beef hard, then build the sauce on shacha, garlic and ginger in the same pan. Makansutra stir-fries everything together with chilies and a splash of rice wine; the lead keeps the beef separate so it stays tender, and this follows the lead. The list calls this a beef-and-greens dish, but the source's greens are scallions only, so nothing else was added. Shacha sauce brands often contain dried fish or shrimp, which is normal for the dish.
